concepts.title: Photographer Bias
concepts.one_liner: The photographer bias is probably one of the most common biases in image databases, and surprisingly difficult to get rid of it.
concepts.content:
### Photographer Bias

The photographer bias is probably one of the most common biases in image databases, and surprisingly difficult to get rid of it.

In a beautiful study, Steve Palmer et al @Palmer1981 showed participants photographs of objects with different orientations in order to measure what orientations they preferred. For each object there were 12 different orientations. Participants had consistent preferences for particular viewpoints for each object. Interestingly, those preferences also correlated with how easy it was to recognize each object.

In another experiment from the same study, participants were shown one picture and their task was to classify the object as quickly as possible from a fixed set of twelve known possible classes. The average response time and accuracy were measured for each of the $12 \times 12$ images. The speed and accuracy are a measure of how easy it is to recognize an object under a particular viewpoint. The study showed that people recognized objects better when presented in a canonical orientation.

@fig-bias_and_shift-palmer_1981enhanced shows the preferred viewpoint for the 12 objects studied.

(see figure: Cannonical viewpoints for 12 objects. Figure from @Palmer1981)

The views that are recognized faster also match the viewpoints that are preferred when taking a picture of those objects @Palmer1981. Such photographer preferred viewpoint introduces biases on how objects are captured, and this bias makes the statistics of object pose in photographs different from the statistics of how objects are actually seen.

The photographer bias exists for objects and scenes (composed of many objects). When taking pictures of scenes, there are biases on the preferred viewpoint, camera orientation (e.g., the horizon is usually inside the picture frame), object locations (such as the one third rule), object arrangements, positions of shadows, types of occlusions, position of the sun, time of day, weather, and so on. All of those factors are taken in consideration (consciously or not) by photographers when deciding which pictures to take.

When building a benchmark, especially when it is small, it is easy to introduce another photographer bias which is to take pictures that "feel" easier to recognize. This might be the right thing to do at first, when debugging a system, but, if abused, has the risk of leading us in the wrong direction when choosing which approach works best.
concepts.motivation_md: Photographer bias affects how objects and scenes are captured, causing datasets to reflect preferred viewpoints rather than how objects are actually seen, which can mislead model training and evaluation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Photographer bias is common and hard to eliminate in image databases.
- People recognize objects faster in canonical orientations, influencing preferred viewpoints.
- Photographer bias affects object pose statistics and scene composition in images.

concepts.title: Collection Bias
concepts.one_liner: There are many potential data sources, all with different biases; Egocentric videos, internet images, vacation photographs, video captured from a moving vehicle, etc.
concepts.content:
### Collection Bias

There are many potential data sources, all with different biases; egocentric videos, internet images, vacation photographs, video captured from a moving vehicle, etc. The potential biases from each data source can be quite significant, and it's often straightforward to identify the capture technique merely by examining the images in a dataset.

@fig-bias_and_shift-mugs shows the first 22 images returned by Google for the query "mug." It looks far from a diverse and unbiased collection of images. As you can appreciate these pictures of mugs look very different from the visual settings in which one usually encounters mugs (inside cabinets, on top of a table, inside the dishwasher, or dirty inside the sink). Instead the images that appear in the search are taken against a flat background, mostly just white, and under a very canonical point of view. For instance, there are no views directly from above.

Other biases can be a bit subtle, for example, most of the handles appear on the right side, and most of the mugs are fully visible, without any occlusions from hands or other objects, and the only two cases of occlusions from mugs occluded by another mug.

(see figure: Pictures of mugs returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.)

The example of the mug, although a bit of a caricature, helps to understand some of the biases that come from the particular collection protocol used to collect images. In this case, images on the internet have a particular type of bias (at least of the ones that get returned under specific searches).

@fig-bias_and_shift-horses shows images returned when looking for "horse." Interestingly many of the pictures are similar to the horse canonical orientation shown in @fig-bias_and_shift-palmer_1981enhanced.

(see figure: Pictures of horses returned by a Google image search. There are many types of biases present in this small image collection.)
concepts.motivation_md: Different data sources introduce distinct biases, making datasets unrepresentative of real-world diversity and affecting model generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Different data sources have distinct biases, e.g., egocentric videos vs. internet images.
- Internet images often show objects in canonical views and clean backgrounds.
- Subtle biases include object orientation and occlusion patterns in collected images.

concepts.title: Annotation Bias
concepts.one_liner: When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use.
concepts.content:
### Annotation Bias

When annotating images, image annotators will choose which images to annotate and which labels to use. This will also correlate with viewpoint preferences and other photographer biases as those images might be easier to annotate and segment, and this has the risk of compounding with the photographer bias.
concepts.motivation_md: Annotation bias arises because annotators select images and labels, often favoring easier viewpoints, which compounds photographer bias and affects dataset representativeness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Annotators choose which images and labels to use.
- Choices correlate with viewpoint and photographer biases.
- This can compound existing biases in datasets.

concepts.title: Social Bias
concepts.one_liner: Social bias refers to biases associated to how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data.
concepts.content:
### Social Bias

This type of bias can affect both the images and the associated labels. Social bias refers to biases associated to how groups of people might be reflected differently in the data. Social biases can be originated by the data collection protocol or by existing social biases. Images can be captured in certain world regions, or contain stereotypes. Labels can reflect social assumptions and biases. An example of social bias is a dataset of images and labels that associates doctors with males and nurses with females.

These types of biases, besides impacting the overall model performance, can have a negative social impact once they are deployed. It is important to be aware of those biases, and incorporate techniques to mitigate their effects. Now it is a good moment for the reader to revisit @sec-computer_vision_and_society.
concepts.motivation_md: Social bias in datasets reflects and perpetuates stereotypes and social assumptions, impacting model fairness and societal outcomes.
concepts.recap_md:
- Social bias affects images and labels reflecting group stereotypes.
- Biases may arise from collection protocols or existing societal biases.
- Such biases can harm model fairness and have negative social impacts.

concepts.title: Testing and Benchmark Bias
concepts.one_liner: One usually thinks about the biases in the training set, but biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on the final system behavior than the training bias.
concepts.content:
### Testing and Benchmark Bias

One usually thinks about the biases in the training set, but biases in the test set can have an even more negative impact on the final system behavior than the training bias. The test set is what researchers and engineers use to decide which algorithm is best, or what data collection is more effective for training. However, there might be little correlation between the performance measured on the test set and the final performance of the system during deployment.

In particular, if we compare two training datasets, one biased and another less biased, by evaluating the performance of a system trained on them using a biased test dataset, we could reach the conclusion that the biased dataset is better.
concepts.motivation_md: Biases in test sets can mislead evaluation and model selection, causing poor real-world performance despite good test results.
concepts.recap_md:
- Test set biases can impact system behavior more than training biases.
- Test sets guide algorithm and data collection choices.
- Biased test sets can falsely favor biased training datasets.

concepts.title: Adversarial Shifts
concepts.one_liner: The data shift is not just random but adversarial, occurring when a competing agent controls the test setting, such as a hacker or a trader.
concepts.content: The data shifts described previously may be disconcerting, but at least they are not malicious. Unfortunately, things can get worse. Quite often the data shift is not just random but adversarial. This may come up whenever our test setting is under the control of a competing agent, for example, someone trying to hack our system (computer security), another animal trying to eat us (evolution), or a trader trying to outperform us on the stock market (finance).
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial shifts arise when data changes are controlled by a competing agent, posing challenges beyond random shifts and requiring robust defenses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial shifts occur when data changes are controlled by an adversary.
- Examples include hackers, predators, or competing traders.
- These shifts are more challenging than random data shifts.

concepts.title: adversarial attacks
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks add imperceptible noise to inputs to fool neural net classifiers into producing any output the attacker desires.
concepts.content:
This was famously demonstrated by @szegedy2014intriguing, who showed that one can add imperceptible noise to an image that fools neural net classifiers despite looking completely innocuous to a human. In fact, the noise pattern can be selected to force the network to produce any output the attacker desires. These are called **adversarial attacks** because we suppose the attacker, who adds the noise, is an adversary that wants to fool or manipulate your system. The adversary can do this by simply optimizing the noise pattern to cause the network to make a particular output, while restricting the noise to be very subtle (within an small $r$-radius ball around the original image). For example, to cause an image classifier $f$ to think the cat in @fig-bias_and_shift-adversarial_perturbation is an ostrich, the attacker could find the noise pattern via the following optimization:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{\epsilon}} H(\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{ostrich}}, f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{\epsilon})), \quad\quad \text{subject to} \quad\quad \left\lVert\mathbf{\epsilon}\right\rVert < r
\end{aligned}$$ where $H$ is the cross-entropy loss and

(see figure: An adversarial attack that adds subtle changes to the cat photo to make a neural net classify it instead as an ostrich. The noise image color values are scaled 20x for visualization.)
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial attacks reveal vulnerabilities in neural networks by showing how subtle noise can manipulate outputs, highlighting the need for robust defenses.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial attacks add subtle noise imperceptible to humans.
- The noise is optimized to force a specific incorrect output.
- Example: fooling a cat classifier into labeling an ostrich.

concepts.title: Adversarial attacks require access to the system to optimize noise patterns
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks require that the attacker has access to the system to optimize noise patterns that fool it.
concepts.content: This type of attack required that the attacker has access to your system (the neural net $f$) so that they can optimize the noise pattern $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ to fool the system. Unfortunately, if you want to deploy your system to the public, then you have to give people access to it and that makes it vulnerable to attack.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that adversarial attacks need system access explains why public deployment increases vulnerability, motivating secure design.

- Adversarial attacks need access to the model to optimize noise.
- Attackers optimize $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ to fool the system.
- Public deployment increases vulnerability to such attacks.

concepts.title: Adversarial attacks are the result of an optimization procedure producing imperceptible noise causing system failure
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial attacks result from optimization procedures that produce imperceptible noise causing system failure with high confidence.
concepts.content: In @sec-neural_nets we described a simple neural network for line classification and showed how, by accessing the architecture and the learned filters, we could manually design input examples that would get wrongly classified. Similarly, in @sec-downsampling_and_upsampling we showed how aliasing could also create vulnerabilities in a network. For large systems, adversarial attacks are not manually designed, instead they are the result of an optimization procedure that optimizes the noise pattern $\mathbf{\epsilon}$ so that it has a small amplitude (i.e., it is imperceptible) and makes the system fail with high confidence.
concepts.motivation_md: Adversarial attacks arise from optimization that finds subtle noise patterns causing confident misclassifications, highlighting systemic vulnerabilities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Small neural networks can be manually fooled by crafted inputs.
- Aliasing can also cause vulnerabilities.
- Large systems face adversarial attacks from optimized imperceptible noise.

concepts.title: Adversarial analysis is worst case analysis and minimizing worst-case error can improve adversarial robustness
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial analysis is worst case analysis, and minimizing worst-case error can improve adversarial robustness.
concepts.content:
Adversarial analysis is worst case analysis. Remember that we typically train our systems to minimize empirical risk, defined as the *mean* error over the training data. Because we only focus on the mean, the *worst case* might be arbitrarily bad. Alternative approaches try to minimize worst-case error, and this can result in systems that are more **adversarially robust**. 

In @sec-data_augmentation we will discuss how **adversarial training** can be used to increase the robustness of the models to adversarial attacks.
concepts.motivation_md: Since typical training minimizes average error, worst-case errors can be large; adversarial analysis focuses on minimizing worst-case error to enhance robustness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial analysis focuses on worst-case errors.
- Typical training minimizes mean error, ignoring worst cases.
- Minimizing worst-case error improves adversarial robustness.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks on dataset bias and shift and approaches to reduce their impact
concepts.one_liner: Dataset bias and shift can be reduced by rigorous data collection, domain randomization, and transfer learning, but bias remains a persistent challenge.
concepts.content:
One way to reduce the issues of dataset bias and shift is to implement a rigorous data collection procedure that tries to minimize the biases present in the data. Although it is possible to prevent (or reduce) certain forms of bias, others will remain challenging because it is hard to collect the necessary data or because we are not aware of it. In many cases, deployment will be done in specific settings that might be unknown a priori. Therefore, bias is here to stay and it is important to study forms to reduce its methods in the system performance.

There are two general ways of dealing with dataset bias and shift. The first is called domain randomization, or data augmentation. The second is called transfer learning, or model adaptation. The next two chapters are about these options.
concepts.motivation_md: Bias and shift in datasets affect system performance; understanding methods like data augmentation and transfer learning helps mitigate these issues.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rigorous data collection can reduce but not eliminate bias.
- Bias persists due to unknown or hard-to-collect data.
- Domain randomization and transfer learning address bias and shift.

concepts.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization
concepts.motivation_md: Out-of-distribution generalization studies how models perform on data distributions different from training, aiming to improve robustness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Out-of-distribution generalization concerns model performance on unseen distributions.
- It is key for deploying models in real-world scenarios.
- Research focuses on methods to improve robustness.

concepts.title: A Toy Example
aliases: toy example for bias and shift
concepts.one_liner: A toy example illustrates the effect of training on one dataset and testing on another with different data distributions.
concepts.content:
Let's start by looking at a toy example. In this toy example, we consider two datasets, each with different data distributions. We study the effect of training on one dataset and testing on another.

Observations $(x,y)$ are sampled from a distribution where $x$ is sampled from a Gaussian and $y$ are noisy observations of the function $f$ applied to $x$:

$$\begin{aligned}
    x &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma) \\
    y & = f(x) + \beta \epsilon \\
    \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)
\end{aligned}$$

The unknown function $f$ has the form:

$$f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_0 x + \theta_1 x^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{hypothesis space}$$

In the first dataset, the Gaussian parameters are $\mu_A = -1.5$, and the standard deviation is $\sigma_A = 1.5$. In the second dataset, the Gaussian has $\mu_B = 2.5$ and $\sigma_B = 0.5$.

For each dataset, we sample two sets of examples: a training set and a test set, which we use to measure generalization error.

Learning is done by optimizing the loss over the corresponding training set:

$$J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left\lVert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right\rVert_2^2 + \lambda \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{objective}$$

@fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets shows training and test examples from both datasets and illustrates the effect of training on one dataset and testing on another. Each plot shows the training samples (circles), used to fit the model, and test samples (triangles) used to measure the generalization error. The diagonal plots show the training and test set corresponding to distribution A, @fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets (top-left), and distribution B, @fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets (bottom-right). In each case, the fitted model is shown as a dashed line.

(see figure: Training and testing on different datasets. In this illustration, all datasets have 5 samples.)

When training and testing is done using samples from the same distribution (A to A, or B to B) the learned model (best fit) passes near the test samples and the error is small. However, when training and test are coming from different distributions, the error can be large. @tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets shows the generalization error made with different combinations of training and test sets as shown in @fig-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets.

| Training set | Test set A | Test set B |
|--------------|------------|------------|
| A            | 0.18       | 0.7        |
| B            | 1.93       | 0.23       |
: Generalization error for different combinations of training and test sets. {#tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets}

The diagonal elements correspond to the error obtained when training on the training examples of dataset A and testing on the test examples of dataset A, and when training and testing on dataset B.

As shown in @tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets, the error becomes larger for the elements off-diagonal. However, @tbl-bias_and_shift-training_test_sets only gives a partial picture about what is happening because it gives the error only for dataset size equal to 5. What happens if we add more data?

It is interesting in general to look at the performance as a function of training data. If we add more data, does performance improve when training and testing on different datasets? Or does it saturate? The answer will depend on the form of the data distributions and the hypothesis space. But we can check what happens in this toy example.

@fig-bias_and_shift-test_as_function_of_data plots the generalization error (vertical axis) when evaluating on dataset A as a function of the amount of training data (horizontal axis).

(see figure: Generalization error as a function of number of training examples. Test set is dataset A. Each curve shows the performance when training with dataset A and with dataset B (same distributions as in...)

Interestingly, both training sets (A and B) succeed in reducing the generalization error on the test set of dataset A when more training data is available. In this example, even the biased dataset B is still able to train a successful model of dataset A. However, the reduction of the error is slower than when training on dataset A. Examples from dataset B are less valuable than examples from dataset A @Torralba2011. We need approximately 10 times more examples from dataset B in order to reach a particular performance. Another way of saying this is that the value of a training example from dataset B when evaluating on dataset A is around $1/10$ of the value of a sample from A.
concepts.motivation_md: This toy example illustrates how training on one data distribution and testing on another affects generalization error, highlighting the impact of data bias and distribution shift.
concepts.recap_md:
- Training and testing on the same distribution yields low error; cross-distribution testing increases error.
- More training data generally reduces error, but biased datasets require more samples.
- The value of samples depends on their distribution relative to the test set.

prereq.rationale: The idea that adversarial attacks require access to the system builds directly on the definition of adversarial attacks involving optimizing noise patterns.
prereq.semantic_review: The idea that adversarial attacks require access to the system to optimize noise patterns is directly supported by the passage stating the attacker must have access to the neural net to optimize the noise. This is a direct dependency, so 'requires' is correct.

prereq.rationale: The optimization procedure producing imperceptible noise causing system failure is a key mechanism described in the definition of adversarial attacks.
prereq.semantic_review: The idea that adversarial attacks result from an optimization procedure producing imperceptible noise causing system failure is directly supported by the text. This optimization procedure is a key mechanism in the definition of adversarial attacks, so 'requires' is appropriate.

prereq.rationale: Adversarial analysis as worst-case analysis builds on the concept of adversarial shifts, focusing on minimizing worst-case error for robustness.
prereq.semantic_review: The idea that adversarial analysis is worst-case analysis and minimizing worst-case error improves robustness builds on the concept of adversarial shifts, which describe adversarial data shifts. The text supports this dependency, so 'requires' is correct.

prereq.rationale: Annotation bias compounds with photographer bias as annotators tend to choose images and labels influenced by photographer viewpoint preferences, thus understanding annotation bias requires understanding photographer bias.
prereq.semantic_review: The passage explicitly states that annotation bias correlates with and compounds with photographer bias, indicating a direct dependency. Understanding annotation bias requires understanding photographer bias, so 'requires' is appropriate.

overlay.rationale: Understanding adversarial attacks requires knowing about adversarial shifts, since attacks exploit malicious data shifts.
overlay.semantic_review: The adversarial attacks definition describes adding imperceptible noise to fool classifiers, and the adversarial shifts concept describes the nature of adversarial data shifts. While adversarial attacks exploit adversarial shifts, the text does not explicitly state that understanding adversarial attacks requires understanding adversarial shifts. The relation is more associative than a strict prerequisite, so 'see_also' is a better edge kind than 'requires'.
